newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-RESEARCH ALERT - BHP faces hardship.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-RESEARCH ALERT - BHP faces hardship.

text.p: Australian resources giant The Broken Hill Proprietary Co Ltd (BHP) faces another six to 12 months of difficulty and is likely to underperform for the rest of calendar 1996, brokerage J.B. Were and Son said.

In a research report dated August 1996, the brokerage recommended investors' share portfolios be underweight in BHP stock in the short term, but said profits and the group's share price were likely to pick up from 1997.

The report, prepared by analyst Neil Goodwill, said continuing strong price competition in BHP's steel business, falling copper pricies and expected lower oil sales were behind the near-term weakness seen for BHP.

"We recommend holding BHP underweight for the next six to nine months and, while it may benefit from overall resource sector support, we believe better gains would be made in other leading miners, such as WMC Ltd and RTZ-CRA," the report said.
But, in the longer term, the report recommended investors' portfolios become overweight in BHP shares.

"BHP has repositioned its business, both in terms of product mix and geographic diversification, and while in the short term this may have exposed the company to some degree of volatility of earnings, longer term it will allow the company to benefit from growth opportunities throughout the world," Were said.
"Their entry into new business across a range of commodities, while providing some start-up risk, will provide the platforms for future substantial growth opportunities beyond 2000," it added.
The report praised BHP's performance over the past 14 months, noting the group had turned around its steel division and shown "outstanding" success in its minerals division.
But two consecutive poor quarterly results have dampened market sentiment toward the stock, the report said.

"Until the market sees confirmation of a pick-up in profits through a (domestic) housing-led recovery in steel, and gains confidence in the profits generated by the raft of new projects due to commence from 1997 onwards, we would expect the company to underperform," it said.

But J.B. Were described the recent disappointing results as part of the volatility to be expected from such a high-growth company, and forecast an earnings recovery in the year to May 31, 1997 and sustained profit growth from 1997/98.

It forecast a net profit before abnormals in 1996/97 of A$1.64 billion -- roughly level with 1995 earnings -- and a 1997/98 net profit of A$1.85 billion. In 1995/96, BHP reported a 20 percent fall in pre-abnormal net profit to A$1.29 billion.
BHP shares closed six cents higher at A$16.84 on Monday. The stock has traded between A$15.90 and A$20.05 this year.
